title: Which number is bigger in each pair?
description: Four pairs of numbers, each given with a unit like thousand, lakh, million, crore or billion, are written in full and compared by their digits. Each pair is then checked by writing both numbers in the same unit.
teaching_notes: One idea: a unit hides the size, so write each number in full with its zeros and compare the digit counts first. Ask the class how many zeros a lakh has before any pair is compared. Watch for students who compare thirty with three and ignore the units.

video_script.why: The child knows the zeros in a thousand, lakh, crore, million and billion, and now uses them to compare numbers given with different units.
video_script.substitution: Write each number in full as its count times the zeros of its unit, compare the digit counts, then check by writing both in the same unit.
video_script.anchor: Four pairs of numbers, each with a unit name, and a blank sign between the two numbers of every pair.
video_script.payoff_line: Each pair now has its sign

final_answer.spoken: less than, greater than, less than, less than

never_show: a sign between the numbers of a pair before the answer beat
maths_rules: zeros: thousand 3, lakh 5, million 6, crore 7, billion 9
30 thousand = 30 × 1000 = 30,000 (5 digits); 3 lakhs = 3 × 1,00,000 = 3,00,000 (6 digits); fewer digits, so 30 thousand < 3 lakhs
800 thousand = 800 × 1000 = 8,00,000 (6 digits); 8 million = 8 × 10,00,000 = 80,00,000 (7 digits); so 800 thousand < 8 million
check in the same unit: 3 lakhs = 300 thousand > 30 thousand; 5 million = 50 lakhs < 500 lakhs; 800 thousand = 8 lakhs < 80 lakhs = 8 million; 60 billion = 6000 crore > 640 crore
video_script.design: One idea: write each number in full with its zeros and compare the digits. The anchor stays all video; the working band builds in the idea part; no hard clear.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, write both numbers of a pair in full. Thirty times one thousand has five digits.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Three times one lakh has six digits. Fewer digits means a smaller number, so thirty thousand is smaller.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Five hundred times one lakh has eight digits. Five times one million has seven digits.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>More digits means a bigger number, so five hundred lakhs is bigger.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, in the next pair, eight hundred times one thousand has six digits.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Eight times one million has seven digits, so eight hundred thousand is smaller.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Six hundred forty times one crore has ten digits.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Sixty times one billion has eleven digits, so six hundred forty crore is smaller.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: check in one unit: 3 lakhs = 300 thousand, more than 30 thousand; 5 million = 50 lakhs, less than 500 lakhs; 800 thousand = 8 lakhs, 8 million = 80 lakhs; 60 billion = 6000 crore, more than 640 crore

marks.m1: both numbers of each pair are rewritten in one unit
marks.m2: 300 thousand beside 30 thousand, and 50 lakhs beside 500 lakhs
marks.m3: 8 lakhs beside 80 lakhs, and 640 crore beside 6000 crore

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, check by writing both numbers of a pair in the same unit.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Three lakhs is three hundred thousand, which is more than thirty thousand. Five million is fifty lakhs, which is less than five hundred lakhs.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Eight hundred thousand is eight lakhs, and eight million is eighty lakhs. Sixty billion is six thousand crore, which is more than six hundred forty crore.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 30 thousand < 3 lakhs; 500 lakhs > 5 million; 800 thousand < 8 million; 640 crore < 60 billion

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Each pair now has its sign.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Thirty thousand is less than three lakhs. Five hundred lakhs is greater than five million.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Eight hundred thousand is less than eight million. Six hundred forty crore is less than sixty billion.
